title: Blood Routes
dek: 312 people died in 12 days during the 2025 Eid-ul-Adha rush. Bangladesh's roads kill at six times the official count. The joma incentive system, political shields, and four critical data voids make it structural — not accidental.
summary: A scroll-driven visual investigation into nationwide road crash fatalities in Bangladesh: the Eid holiday surge, the joma economic machine that incentivises racing, the Phoenix rebrand pattern, and four data voids the government holds but refuses to publish.
key_findings: During the 12-day Eid-ul-Adha 2025 travel period, 312 people were killed — a 29% year-on-year surge in holiday fatalities, averaging 26 deaths per day.
The WHO-modelled road death estimate (~31,578/year) is 5.8× higher than the BRTA official count (5,480) — a gap maintained by deliberate policy, not technical incapacity.

The joma (daily deposit) system forces bus drivers to race for passengers under a guaranteed-income model that protects owners and transfers all lethal risk to drivers and pedestrians, 47% of Dhaka victims.

title: The Lead Belt
dek: Bangladesh's lead poisoning crisis mapped: 294 contaminated sites, 145 schools within 500 metres, and soil lead readings up to 1,702 times the international safety standard.
summary: A forensic spatial investigation mapping contaminated lead sites, nearby schools, child exposure indicators, and state inaction across Bangladesh.
key_findings: 294 contaminated sites are mapped across Bangladesh using Pure Earth / University of Dhaka assessment data.
145 schools are identified within 500 metres of contaminated sites, with the closest school in the report sitting 59 metres from a lead-acid battery recycling site.
The highest soil lead reading in the report reaches 680,872 ppm, about 1,702 times the 400 ppm international residential safety threshold.

title: The Impunity Machine
dek: A visual data investigation into Bangladesh's rape justice crisis and the institutional machinery that turns reported violence into near-zero punishment.
summary: A forensic visual investigation tracing Bangladesh's rape justice crisis across reporting attrition, conviction rates, court backlog, forensic capacity, and legal data voids.
key_findings: Only 310 convictions were recorded from 66,711 women who came through One-Stop Crisis Centres over 23 years, a 0.46% conviction rate.
Bangladesh pairs maximum legal severity with near-zero certainty of punishment: death penalty expansion did not solve reporting attrition, backlog, evidence loss, or witness risk.
Critical justice infrastructure remains thin: 14 OCCs, two national DNA machines, major unprocessed sample backlogs, and no complete national registry for key rape-case outcomes.
